title: Element 2: How Health & Safety Management Systems Work
learningObjectives: Describe the key elements of a health and safety management system (HSMS)
Explain the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle and its application to H&S management
Outline the content and purpose of a health and safety policy
Describe the role of worker consultation and participation in H&S management

content.text: What is a Health and Safety Management System?

A Health and Safety Management System (HSMS) is a structured framework for managing safety risks within an organisation. Rather than dealing with hazards as they arise, an HSMS provides systematic, proactive processes for identifying hazards, assessing risks, implementing controls, and continually improving performance.

The three main HSMS frameworks you need to know: ILO-OSH 2001 (ILO Occupational Safety and Health Management Systems Guidelines), ISO 45001:2018 (international standard), and HSG65 (UK HSE's 'Managing for Health and Safety').
All major HSMS frameworks are based on the PDCA cycle, sometimes called the Deming cycle. This cycle represents the principle of continual improvement.

rows: PLAN
Set objectives, identify hazards, assess risks, plan controls
H&S policy, risk assessments, emergency plans, training plans
DO
Implement the planned controls and safe systems of work
Running toolbox talks, issuing permits, providing PPE, conducting training
CHECK
Monitor, measure, and audit performance against objectives
Inspections, audits, incident investigation, reviewing statistics
ACT
Review findings and take corrective and preventive action
Closing out audit findings, revising procedures, updating risk assessments

content.text: ISO 45001 (the international OHSMS standard) is explicitly based on the PDCA cycle. Many Gulf companies — particularly those aligned with Aramco SEMP or ADNOC's HSEMS — require their contractors to demonstrate PDCA-based HSMS. This is a common topic in Gulf QHSE interviews.

A H&S policy is a formal statement of an organisation's commitment to managing health and safety. Most legal frameworks require employers above a certain size to have a written policy. It must be signed by the most senior person in the organisation (e.g., CEO, Managing Director).
The policy has three distinct sections:

rows: Statement of Intent
Overall commitment to H&S; objectives; general philosophy
Most senior person — CEO/MD
Organisation
Roles and responsibilities at each level — who is accountable for what
All managers referenced
Arrangements
Specific procedures for managing key H&S issues (risk assessment, training, PPE, etc.)
H&S manager/director

content.text: A policy that is not communicated is worthless. Workers must be able to access and understand it. It must also be reviewed regularly — at least annually and after significant changes in the organisation.
Effective organisation for H&S requires four elements, often remembered as the '4 Cs':

items: Control — Clear lines of responsibility; defined roles for H&S at all levels; accountability
Cooperation — All members of the organisation work together; team approach; joint H&S committees
Communication — Effective two-way communication of H&S information (toolbox talks, notices, procedures)
Competence — All workers have the skills, knowledge, and experience to carry out their roles safely; training

content.text: Worker consultation is not optional — it is both a legal requirement and a practical necessity. Workers have direct knowledge of workplace hazards that managers may lack. Effective consultation means giving workers enough information to make a meaningful contribution, and genuinely considering their input.

items: Safety Representatives — Appointed by recognised trade unions; have specific legal rights
H&S Committees — Joint employer-worker forums to discuss H&S matters; must be established when requested by safety reps
Direct Consultation — Non-unionised workplaces: employer consults workers directly or through elected representatives
Toolbox Talks — Short, focused pre-shift safety briefings; excellent for daily communication

content.text: A refinery is planning to introduce a new chemical cleaning process. The H&S committee is consulted during the planning phase. Workers who will carry out the process identify a practical issue with the proposed PPE in hot conditions. Their input leads to a change in procedure that protects workers and avoids a costly post-implementation rework.
Planning in an HSMS involves setting measurable H&S objectives and targets. These should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

items: Leading indicators — Proactive measures of safety activity (number of inspections conducted, % of training completed, near-miss reports submitted)
Lagging indicators — Reactive measures of safety outcomes (injury rates, TRCR, LTIFR, days lost)
Benchmarking — Comparing your performance against industry peers or previous periods

content.text: The number of Lost Time Injuries per million hours worked. Formula: (Number of LTIs × 1,000,000) ÷ Total hours worked. Standard measure used across Gulf O&G and construction.

Aramco requires monthly HSE statistics from all contractors: Total Recordable Case Rate (TRCR), Days Away from Work Rate (DAFWR), and Near Miss Rate. Poor statistics trigger contractor performance reviews and can result in contract termination. Understanding how to calculate and report these statistics is essential for any Gulf HSE professional.
